content.title: Optimise Review Latency, Not Review Depth
content.text:
Engineering teams talk about code review as if the goal were to catch bugs. Reviewers are encouraged to be thorough, to pull the branch and run it, to leave detailed comments. I want to argue that this framing is mostly wrong for most teams, and that the number worth watching is how long a change waits for review, not how carefully it is read once someone gets to it.

Begin with what review actually catches. The Calloway Software Institute published a defect-escape analysis in 2025 that traced 3,400 production bugs across nine companies back to the change that introduced them and then to the review that approved that change. For each bug, they asked whether the review had left any comment on the lines that turned out to be defective. The answer was yes in 11 percent of cases. In the other 89 percent, the defective lines drew no comment at all, regardless of how many comments the review contained overall. Reviews with more than ten comments were no more likely to have touched the defective lines than reviews with two. The reviewers who did catch bugs were disproportionately the ones who owned the affected code, not the ones who spent the most time.

This is roughly what you would expect. Reviewers are good at spotting confusing names, missing tests, and style deviations. They are poor at mentally executing a change against production data and concurrency. The bugs that escape are the ones that require running the code, which is what tests and staging environments are for.

Now consider what review latency costs. The same institute's cycle-time data, drawn from 61,000 pull requests, shows that the median time from a change being opened to first review was 19 hours, and from first review to merge another 26 hours. Author time spent writing the change was a median of 4 hours. In other words, a change spent about ten times as long waiting as being written. Every hour of that wait is an hour in which the author has switched to something else, the branch drifts from main, and the eventual merge conflict or rebase introduces exactly the kind of mistake the review will not catch.

The latency effect on defects is measurable. The Calloway analysis grouped changes by time-to-first-review and found that changes reviewed within four hours had a defect-escape rate of 2.1 percent; changes that waited more than 48 hours had a rate of 4.6 percent. The authors controlled for change size and concluded that the difference was driven mostly by rebase conflicts and by authors having lost context by the time reviewer questions arrived.

Delphine Aubert, an engineering manager, changed her team's review norms around this finding. The team of eleven agreed that any review request would be acknowledged within two hours during working time, that a reviewer who could not do a full read would do a fast one and say so, and that changes over 400 lines would be sent back to be split. Over two quarters, median time-to-first-review fell from 22 hours to 2.5. Merged changes per engineer per week rose from 3.1 to 5.4. Bugs attributed to recently merged changes, tracked in their incident tool, fell slightly, from 7 per month to 5. Her team's own explanation was that smaller, faster changes were easier to review well, so speed and depth had turned out not to be in tension at all.

I will concede the situations where depth matters. Changes to authentication, billing, or data migration deserve a slow, careful read and probably a second reviewer, and no latency target should override that. Codebases with weak test coverage lean harder on human review by necessity, and the right fix there is the tests, not faster approvals. And a review culture can become so fast that it is rubber-stamping; the Calloway authors note a small cluster of teams with sub-hour review times and above-average escape rates, which they attribute to approvals without reading.

But those are edge cases against a strong central pattern. For the ordinary change on an ordinary day, the review that arrives in an hour and says it looks fine with one question does more good than the one that arrives in two days with fifteen comments. Measure your queue. If changes are sitting for a day, that is your most expensive quality problem, and it is a scheduling problem, not a diligence problem.

notes: Opinion piece arguing review wait time matters more than review thoroughness, backed by a fictional defect-escape analysis and cycle-time dataset with concrete rates, a named manager's before/after results, and clear carve-outs for high-risk changes. Judge should treat this as substantive, evidence-led argument.
